passage: Noor had taught at the same Malappuram primary school for three years, and lately every day felt like the same grey photocopy. In March she decided to change one thing. On Saturdays she began helping at the panchayat library, sorting donated books and reading aloud to the smallest children. Her colleague Thomas, who ran it, gave her the dustiest shelf. By May she was staying past closing, laughing at the children's questions. But some mornings the heaviness still sat on her chest before she even got up, and it had been going on since winter. One Monday she took half a day off, caught the bus into town and sat in the clinic waiting room with a token in her hand. Library on Saturday. Doctor on Monday. Both, she decided.

qa.q: Where did Noor help on Saturdays?
qa.a: At the panchayat library.

qa.q: What was Noor feeling on the mornings the heaviness sat on her chest?
qa.a: Noor felt weighed down even before the day began, a heaviness the library eased but didn't fully lift.

qa.q: Why was Noor's choice of "both" a wise one?
qa.a: The library added meaning and joy, while seeing a doctor dealt with a heaviness that had lasted since winter, instead of waiting it out.

qa.q: How might the smallest children at the library see Noor?
qa.a: The children likely see a warm reader who laughs at their questions, and look forward to Saturdays.

grounding: A small-town teacher adds weekend library service to her life and, because the heaviness has lasted, also sees a doctor.

passage: By July, Zanele's weeks in Johannesburg had flattened into one long Tuesday: taxi, spreadsheet, taxi, television. Nothing was wrong enough to complain about. So she changed the pattern on purpose. She swapped her lunchtime scrolling for a walk to the community garden two streets from the office, where an old man named Sipho grew spinach in tyres. He handed her a trowel on the second day. On Saturdays she started a beginners' woodwork class with her friend Omar, who made a spectacularly crooked stool. Some evenings still went grey. She made herself a promise and wrote it on the fridge: If the grey gets heavier or doesn't lift, book the clinic, don't wait. For now, there was spinach to water.

qa.q: Where did Sipho grow spinach?
qa.a: In tyres at the community garden.

qa.q: What does the note on Zanele's fridge show about Zanele's thinking?
qa.a: It shows Zanele is wary of the grey feeling, taking it seriously and deciding not to just wait it out if it gets heavier.

qa.q: Which of Zanele's changes seems to help most, and why?
qa.a: The garden walks seem to help, since swapping scrolling for time with Sipho and the plants breaks the one-long-Tuesday pattern.

qa.q: How might Sipho see Zanele coming back each lunchtime?
qa.a: Sipho probably enjoys the company and the extra pair of hands, which is why he handed over a trowel on the second day.

grounding: An adult breaks a flat routine with gardening and woodwork, and plans to see the clinic if the grey feeling gets heavier.

passage:
For most of the year, Pema, twenty-six, had felt flat: work, sleep, the same videos. In April she signed up for the Tuesday pottery class at the community centre in Gangtok, mostly because the poster had a messy handprint on it. Varun, the instructor, handed her a lump of clay. "It'll collapse the first ten times. That's the class." It collapsed. She laughed out loud for the first time in weeks. By June she was helping the older ladies centre their clay and staying to sweep up.
But some weeks the heaviness still came back and sat on her for days. So one Tuesday, before class, she stopped at the centre's health desk and booked a session with the visiting counsellor. Pottery helped. She just didn't want to wait and see if it was enough.

qa.q: What did Varun say about the clay?
qa.a: "It'll collapse the first ten times. That's the class."

qa.q: What does Pema's laughing out loud suggest about the class?
qa.a: It suggests the class was bringing back joy and lightness for Pema after weeks of feeling flat.

qa.q: Which two choices did Pema make, and why do both matter?
qa.a: She took up pottery for a new skill and purpose, and booked the counsellor because the heaviness kept returning.

qa.q: How might the older ladies at the class see Pema?
qa.a: They probably see her as a cheerful helper, perhaps without guessing how flat she had been feeling.

grounding: An adult answers months of flatness with a new skill and service, and books a counsellor as it stays heavy.

passage:
Dear Jhanvi,
You asked why I sound more like myself lately. Here's the honest answer.
For about eight months, everything felt flat. Not tragic, just grey. Office, metro, dinner, phone, sleep. I stopped wanting anything.
So I changed one pattern. I started cycling to work twice a week instead of taking the metro. Then I signed up to coach chess on Sunday mornings at the children's library near my flat. Twelve kids, total chaos, one boy who cries every time he loses a knight. I actually look forward to it.
The other thing, and I'm telling you because you're my sister: the flatness was getting heavy, so I went to a doctor, and she referred me to a counsellor. Three sessions so far. I'm not fixed, but I'm not waiting it out alone any more.
Love,
Nitin

qa.q: Where does Nitin coach chess on Sunday mornings?
qa.a: At the children's library near Nitin's flat.

qa.q: How did Nitin feel during those eight months?
qa.a: Nitin felt flat and grey, not tragic but empty of wanting anything, and the flatness slowly grew heavy.

qa.q: Why was going to a doctor a wise step alongside the chess and cycling?
qa.a: Because the flatness had become heavy and lasting, and new activities alone might not be enough; getting help meant not waiting it out.

qa.q: How might Jhanvi feel reading this letter?
qa.a: Jhanvi might feel relieved, proud of her sibling for getting help, and glad to be trusted with it.

grounding: An adult changes routines and takes on coaching, and sees a doctor and counsellor when the flatness grows heavy.
